newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungary says blockade plan illegal, farmers defiant. [CORRECTED 18:57 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Hungary says blockade plan illegal, farmers defiant. [CORRECTED 18:57 GMT]

text.p: A Hungarian farmers' union on Tuesday maintained its threat to block border crossings if the government does not agree to its demands, despite warnings that such action would be illegal.

"We will go ahead with the plan (if our demands are not met)," Gyula Kosa, leader of farmers' union METESZ told Reuters in a telephone interview. "We will organise a series of road-blocks around the country".

METESZ sent an ultimatum to the government on Monday saying it would set up road-blocks at Hungary's border crossings and on roads leading into the capital if its demand, unconditional tax relief for farmers earning less than 1.5 million forints ($8,500) a year, was not met.

Earlier on Tuesday government spokesman Elemer Kiss said METESZ's blockade threat was both illegal and anti-constitutional and added that the union's claims that the government refused to talk were untrue.
"(The union's) opinion that the government refused to negotiate is completely unfounded," he told reporters.
If the farmers carry out their ultimatum, police have the right to remove them from the roads, he added.
Kiss also said Prime Minister Gyula Horn had sent a letter to Jozsef Torgyan, leader of opposition party Smallholders and a supporter of METESZ's actions, asking him to reconsider his position.
A February demonstration in the central Hungarian town of Kiskoros sparked a series of farmers' protests following 1997 income and social security tax increases for individual farmers.

The government made a series of initial concessions to the farmers, who have since formed METESZ. Those concessions are due to be submitted for emergency parliamentary debate this week. (Corrects to make clear that parliament will debate the concessions, not the ultimatum.)

METESZ has asked for further concessions, and analysts believe the move could trigger a chain reaction as larger farmers' unions resort to action to hold onto their increasingly dissatisfied members. (Corrects to make clear union asked for further concessions before issuing its road-block ultimatum.)

Gabor Horvath, general secretary of MOSZ, Hungary's biggest farmers' union, has asked the government to subsidise its members social security contributions by 50 percent out of agricultural subsidy funds.
He did not exclude the possibility of demonstrations by MOSZ's 150,000 members.
"The situation is getting ripe for such a move," Horvath said.
